title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 97–98
description: Reviewed B2 similes and traditional proverbs, with contextual meanings, register notes, and original usage examples.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary targets follow source topics and relevant exercise vocabulary; teaching examples and explanations are independently written. Original textbook exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Both study pages, illustrated comparisons, proverb tables, exercise tasks and relevant answer-key entries checked for target coverage and meaning.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for a small number of short, reliable targets; longer fixed similes and proverbs intentionally leave IPA empty rather than supplying unreliable phonemic transcriptions. Important pronunciation contrasts are explained in notes.
audit.languagePolicy: All strings are in English except natural Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared targets, captions and exercise-only vocabulary with the source and answer key; wrote independent teaching examples; reviewed figurative meaning, register, translation, ID uniqueness, word-audio target wording, and static JSON structure.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio, live VocabLab import, browser TTS, speech recognition, or UI round-trip testing was performed.

units.title: Unit 97 — Similes
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 97. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise fixed as ... as and like similes and infer their figurative meanings.
Distinguish superficially similar expressions, including as sick as a dog versus as sick as a parrot, and as white as snow versus as white as a sheet.
Identify humorous, informal or potentially offensive similes and choose register appropriately.
Associate visual imagery and sound patterns with the source expressions and exercise-only comparisons.

sectionsChecked: A: As ... as and illustrated comparisons
Language help: as ... as can be

items.example: A simile can make an everyday description more vivid.
items.note: An expression comparing two things, often using like or as ... as.

items.pt: mortinho; completamente morto; sem qualquer atividade
items.example: By the end of winter, the neglected plant was as dead as a doornail.
items.note: Strong informal comparison meaning completely dead; figuratively, an organisation or idea may be inactive.

items.pt: cego como um morcego; que enxerga muito mal
items.example: Without my glasses, I am as blind as a bat when reading small labels.
items.note: Humorous but potentially insensitive comparison about poor eyesight; avoid using it about another person without care.

items.example: After weeks of illness, the character looked as thin as a rake.
items.note: Informal appearance comparison that may sound critical or unkind.

items.example: My uncle is as strong as an ox and carried the heavy suitcase upstairs.
items.note: An ox is a large farm animal; often used approvingly for physical strength.

items.example: The children were as quiet as a mouse while they waited backstage.
items.note: Means very quiet and not attracting attention; can describe a person or behaviour.

items.example: The soaked blanket felt as heavy as lead.
items.note: Lead is the metal /led/, not the verb lead /liːd/. Opposite comparison: as light as a feather.

items.example: Despite its size, the empty box was as light as a feather.
items.note: Very light in weight; contrast with as heavy as lead.

items.example: He arrived at the party as drunk as a lord and could barely speak.
items.note: Very informal and critical; traditionally British. Contrasts with as sober as a judge.

items.example: Everyone else had been drinking, but the driver was as sober as a judge.
items.note: Means not under the influence of alcohol; sometimes used humorously.

items.example: The sky above the remote village was as black as night.
items.note: Strong descriptive comparison about darkness.

items.example: The mountain peaks were as white as snow after the storm.
items.note: Often used in traditional stories to describe pure or beautiful whiteness; compare as white as a sheet.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: The twins were as good as gold during the long train journey.
items.note: Used especially to praise children for behaving well.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: Even during the interview, Marta remained as cool as a cucumber.
items.note: Cool here means composed, not cold in temperature.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: The volunteers were as busy as a bee before the festival opened.
items.note: Very active and continuously working; the noun bee creates a memorable sound pattern.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: The old mattress was as hard as iron, so nobody slept well.
items.note: Describes an extremely hard surface, usually negatively in this context.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: After several weeks without rain, the garden soil was as dry as a bone.
items.note: Means completely dry; often describes ground, weather or objects.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: Everyone thought the inventor was as mad as a hatter when he proposed the idea.
items.note: Strong, potentially offensive description of apparently irrational or eccentric behaviour; avoid using as a literal mental-health label.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: He walked into the restricted meeting as bold as brass and demanded an explanation.
items.note: Someone acting with surprising confidence or shamelessness, often disregarding social expectations.

items.pt: com muita dificuldade de ouvir; surdo como uma porta
items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: In the novel, the elderly neighbour is described as deaf as a post.
items.note: Potentially offensive comparison about hearing difficulty; better to use neutral descriptive language about real people.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: Installing the app was as easy as pie once I followed the guide.
items.note: Very informal way of saying something is simple.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: As quick as a flash, the goalkeeper reached the ball.
items.note: Describes an almost immediate action or reaction.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: When he heard the crash, his face turned as white as a sheet.
items.note: Means extremely pale through fear, shock or illness; differs from as white as snow.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: I felt as sick as a dog after eating the spoiled seafood.
items.note: Describes physical illness, often nausea or vomiting; contrast with as sick as a parrot.

items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: The players were as sick as a parrot after losing the final in extra time.
items.note: Informal British expression for deep disappointment rather than physical sickness.

items.pt: vermelho como um tomate; muito corado
items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: When everyone applauded his speech, he went as red as a beetroot.
items.note: Describes a face becoming very red, often through embarrassment; beetroot is British English for the vegetable.

items.pt: com muita sede; sedento ao extremo
items.section: A · As ... as: sound patterns and descriptive phrases
items.example: After the long walk in the heat, we were as thirsty as can be.
items.note: Illustrates the productive pattern as + adjective + as can be, meaning extremely.

items.example: The revised booking system worked like a dream during the launch.
items.note: Means operate very smoothly and successfully. Compare work like a charm in other contexts.

items.pt: ter olhos de águia; não deixar nada passar
items.example: Our proofreader has eyes like a hawk and notices every spelling mistake.
items.note: Describes being exceptionally observant; hawks are birds of prey with sharp eyesight.

items.pt: comer muito; comer como um leão
items.example: My teenage cousin eats like a horse after swimming practice.
items.note: Informal exaggeration for eating large quantities.

items.pt: beber muito álcool; beber como uma esponja
items.example: The character used to drink like a fish before deciding to stop.
items.note: Typically means drink alcohol excessively, not simply drink a lot of water; can sound judgmental.

items.pt: dormir profundamente; dormir feito uma pedra
items.example: I slept like a log after the overnight journey.
items.note: Means sleep very soundly without waking.

items.word: have a mind like a sieve
items.pt: ter memória de peixe; esquecer tudo
items.example: I have a mind like a sieve when it comes to remembering passwords.
items.note: Informal self-description for being forgetful; alternative: have a head like a sieve.

items.word: have a head like a sieve
items.pt: ter memória péssima; viver esquecendo as coisas
items.example: My brother has a head like a sieve and always forgets his keys.
items.note: Variation of have a mind like a sieve; keep word audio separate from the alternative.

items.word: like a bear with a sore head
items.example: The director was like a bear with a sore head after the meeting went badly.
items.note: British informal simile for someone in a very bad mood.

items.word: like a bull in a china shop
items.pt: feito um elefante em loja de cristais; desajeitadamente
items.example: He approached the delicate negotiations like a bull in a china shop.
items.note: Figurative, critical comparison for clumsy or insensitive behaviour; china means porcelain.

items.word: like a red rag to a bull
items.pt: algo que provoca muita irritação; pano vermelho para um touro
items.example: Mentioning that controversial decision was like a red rag to a bull for the committee chair.
items.note: An action or comment is certain to provoke anger.

items.example: The surrounding countryside was as flat as a pancake.
items.note: Common informal comparison for a very flat surface.

items.example: She woke up as fresh as a daisy after a good night’s sleep.
items.note: Used of a person feeling or looking refreshed, not normally of food.

items.example: My hands were as cold as ice after cycling in the rain.
items.note: Can describe literal coldness or, figuratively, lack of warmth or sympathy.

items.word: as easy as falling off a log
items.example: For an experienced carpenter, replacing the hinge was as easy as falling off a log.
items.note: A longer, informal alternative to as easy as pie.

units.title: Unit 98 — Proverbs
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 98. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Understand familiar proverbs as advice, warnings and observations rather than literal claims.
Use a proverb naturally to comment on a relevant situation.
Distinguish proverbs with contrasting messages, such as cooperation versus too much interference.
Recognise the source proverbs and the additional comparisons introduced in the exercises.

sectionsChecked: Language help: Using proverbs in context

items.example: A proverb can summarise an everyday lesson in a memorable sentence.
items.note: A traditional fixed saying giving practical advice, a warning or an observation.

items.word: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
items.pt: não conte com o ovo antes de a galinha botar; não comemore antes da hora
items.example: We haven't signed the contract yet, so don't count your chickens before they hatch.
items.note: Do not assume a hoped-for success will happen; warns against premature certainty.

items.word: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
items.pt: não ponha todos os ovos na mesma cesta; não concentre todos os riscos
items.example: She applied to five universities because she didn't want to put all her eggs in one basket.
items.note: Diversify effort, opportunities or risk rather than relying on only one option.

items.word: Never judge a book by its cover.
items.pt: não julgue um livro pela capa; as aparências enganam
items.example: The tiny restaurant looked unremarkable, but never judge a book by its cover.
items.note: Outer appearance does not reliably reveal a person’s or thing’s true quality.

items.word: Never look a gift-horse in the mouth.
items.pt: cavalo dado não se olha os dentes
items.example: The ticket was free, so I accepted it; never look a gift-horse in the mouth.
items.note: Do not criticise a generous gift or favourable opportunity. The hyphenated spelling is from the source.

items.word: Take care of the pennies and the pounds will take care of themselves.
items.pt: de grão em grão a galinha enche o papo; pequenas economias fazem diferença
items.example: She checks even small subscriptions because she believes that if you take care of the pennies, the pounds will take care of themselves.
items.note: Managing small expenses can lead to substantial savings; pounds and pennies refer to British currency.

items.word: We'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
items.pt: vamos resolver isso quando chegar a hora; cada coisa a seu tempo
items.example: We haven't even been offered the job, so we'll cross that bridge when we come to it.
items.note: Do not spend too much energy worrying about a possible future problem.

items.word: When the cat's away, the mice will play.
items.pt: quando o gato sai, os ratos fazem a festa
items.example: The supervisor left early and everyone relaxed; when the cat's away, the mice will play.
items.note: People may behave more freely when the person in authority is absent.

items.word: You can lead a horse to water but you can't make it drink.
items.pt: você pode mostrar o caminho, mas não pode obrigar alguém a segui-lo
items.example: I sent him the training materials, but he refused to study; you can lead a horse to water but you can't make it drink.
items.note: Advice or opportunities can be offered, but a person cannot be forced to accept them.

items.word: One swallow doesn't make a summer.
items.pt: uma andorinha só não faz verão
items.example: One good sales month is encouraging, but one swallow doesn't make a summer.
items.note: A single positive sign does not prove a long-term improvement; swallow is a migratory bird, not the verb meaning to ingest.

items.example: She doubted the office rumours, but her colleague said there's no smoke without fire.
items.note: Suggests rumours may have some factual basis; it is not proof a particular allegation is true.

items.example: Some people believed the allegations because they thought where there's smoke, there's fire.
items.note: Alternative fixed proverb to there’s no smoke without fire; not reliable evidence by itself.

items.word: People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones.
items.pt: quem tem telhado de vidro não deve atirar pedras no dos outros
items.example: He criticises colleagues for arriving late, although he is always late himself; people who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones.
items.note: Avoid criticising others for faults you also have.

items.word: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
items.pt: muitos chefes atrapalham; cozinheiros demais estragam o caldo
items.example: Five managers rewrote the same report and delayed it for days: too many cooks spoil the broth.
items.note: Too many people interfering in a task can make the result worse; broth means a thin soup.

items.pt: a união faz a força; com ajuda, o trabalho fica mais leve
items.example: The volunteers finished the clean-up in an hour; many hands make light work.
items.note: A task becomes easier when people cooperate; contrast with too many cooks spoil the broth.

items.word: All that glitters is not gold.
items.pt: nem tudo que reluz é ouro
items.example: The offer sounded perfect, but the hidden fees reminded us that all that glitters is not gold.
items.note: Appearances can be misleading; similar in message to never judge a book by its cover.

items.word: Absence makes the heart grow fonder.
items.pt: a distância aumenta a saudade; a ausência fortalece o afeto
items.example: After six months apart, they appreciated each other more; absence makes the heart grow fonder.
items.note: Missing someone or something may deepen affection; contrasts with when the cat’s away, the mice will play.

items.word: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
items.pt: mais vale um pássaro na mão do que dois voando
items.example: She chose the definite job offer over a risky possibility: a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
items.note: A certain benefit may be better than a potentially greater but uncertain one.
